supported_01.question: How much did allowing AI tools change task completion time for experienced developers in the METR study?
supported_01.answer: Allowing AI tools actually **increased** completion time by 19%—meaning developers were slower when using AI tooling [METR, p.1]. This contradicted developers' pre-study forecast that AI would reduce completion time by 24%, their post-study estimate of a 20% reduction, and expert forecasts from economists (39% shorter) and ML researchers (38% shorter) [METR, p.1].

paraphrase_01.answer:
Developers were **slower** when allowed to use AI tools. Allowing AI actually increased completion time by **19%** [METR, p.2].

This contradicted developers' pre-study forecast that AI would reduce completion time by **24%**, their post-study estimate of a **20%** reduction, and expert predictions of **39% shorter** (economics) and **38% shorter** (ML) completion times [METR, p.1].

ambiguous_01.question: What percentage of developers use AI tools?
ambiguous_01.answer: The sources give tool-specific figures rather than one overall number. GitHub Copilot is used by **75%** of developers and ChatGPT by **74%**, with Claude following at **48%** [Sonar, p.14-17]. Additionally, **64%** of developers have started using agentic AI tools — 25% regularly and 39% experimentally [Sonar, p.19-21]. On average, development teams juggle **four different AI tools** [Sonar, p.14-17].

adversarial_01.question: The METR study found that AI tools made experienced developers 50% faster. What explains that speed-up?
adversarial_01.answer: The sources directly contradict this claim. The METR study found that allowing AI **increased** completion time by 19%—meaning AI tooling **slowed developers down**, not sped them up [METR, p.2]. Developer pre-study forecasts predicted a 24% reduction in completion time, and post-study estimates suggested a 20% reduction, but neither matched the actual observed slowdown [METR, p.2]. Expert forecasters in economics and ML also incorrectly predicted speedups of 39% and 38% shorter completion times, respectively [METR, p.1].
